paper_title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Agents that write code to control robots with multimodal language models complete many manipulation tasks zero-shot [12, 15, 19, 29], but preserve nothing from one episode to the next, which makes selfimprovement across episodes natural next step [28, 31, 36]. Such agents are developed and compared on embodied simulation benchmarks [9, 20, 22] originally built to evaluate end-to-end policies trained by imitating demonstrations, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models [4, 6, 17, 25] and world action models (WAMs) [26]. The actual success criteria of these benchmarks often ask for more than the instruction; in the press_by_number task of RoboDojo, for instance, the criteria require the blue button to be pressed exactly twice, between two groups of red presses, which the instruction never states (figure 1a). For policies trained by imitation, this gap is harmless, since their demonstrations already contain every 1 Figure 1 Learning the task or the verifier? (a): in press_by_number, the criteria 𝐶orig verify button protocol that the instruction does not state (highlighted). Without Criteria Exposure (w/o CE) the learner sees only whether each episode succeeded; with it (w/ CE) it also reads the criteria code, score and stages. Right of each setting: the test successes of its library on 20 layouts, judged by 𝐶orig and by the instruction-faithful criteria 𝐶faith. (b): libraries learned under 𝐶orig on the 16 criteria-limited tasks, 320 test episodes each, with every episode judged by both criteria (section 4.2.1). The lead of w/ CE under 𝐶orig, 51.6% against 27.8%, is gone under 𝐶faith (45.0% against 47.2%). detail the criteria verify: order, counts, end states, and the return of both arms. An agent that receives only the instruction, however, lacks this information. Existing self-improving methods therefore expose the criteria to the agent to different degrees, from rule descriptions [10] and published scoring tables [13, 18] to numeric thresholds [14], formal goal predicates [32], and the source code of the verifier [3]. robot in the real world, by contrast, receives only its instruction and, at most, success judged by human or VLM. Our research question is: when self-improving embodied agent is exposed to the success criteria, does the code it iteratively produces better perform the instructed task, or simply overfit to the verification criteria? Studies of benchmark validity and of specification gaming show that criteria can demand more than the instruction states and that agents exploit verifier they can inspect [16, 37, 40], but we are not aware of work that measures how much of reported gain in embodied self-improvement comes from reading the criteria, or whether it survives when the criteria change. We therefore compare two settings of one fixed self-improvement loop, in which frozen coding agent acts and learner agent turns its episodes into library of skills and memory: with Criteria Exposure (w/ CE), the learner reads the criteria; without it (w/o CE), the learner sees only whether each episode succeeded. We ask three questions: on which tasks exposure raises the score; whether its lead survives change of criteria, both of the criteria that judge the episodes and of the criteria the learner reads; and whether what it adds carries over to new tasks and to two further benchmarks, LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365. To change the criteria, we rewrite them for the RoboDojo tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction, so that they verify only what the instruction asks. On these tasks every episode is judged by both versions, and in separate run the learner reads the rewritten criteria instead of the original ones. Our experiments reveal three findings. First, under the original criteria, exposure helps only on tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction; when criteria and instruction agree, learning from success alone does just as well. Second, the score of exposure follows the criteria it read: when the same episodes are judged by instruction-faithful criteria, its advantage disappears, as the exposed libraries lose successes while the success-only libraries gain them (figure 1b); conversely, library learned from the rewritten criteria scores far lower when judged by the original ones. Third, the lead of exposure does not reappear on new RoboDojo tasks, and across benchmarks neither the exposed nor the success-only library gives clear gain over the empty library; only experience gathered within the target benchmark does. Taken together, these results suggest practical principle for evaluating embodied self-improvement: the learner should receive only the feedback robot would receive in the real world, and the benchmarks criteria should verify what the instruction says. gain that holds when the criteria are changed but still agree with the instruction reflects what the agent has learned about the task. Seen this way, whether the learner reads the criteria is not an implementation detail of self-improving agent but choice about 2 measurement, and it determines what reported gain means.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Code-writing embodied agents and their benchmarks. Language models plan and act for robots by selecting skills [1], writing policy code [19], or composing value maps [15]; recent agents close the loop with code replanning and thin tool layers [12, 13, 29], and frontier models now control robots zero-shot. These agents are evaluated on benchmarks built for vision-language-action policies trained on demonstrations [4, 6, 17, 25]: RoboDojo [9], LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO [20, 38], RoboCasa365 [22], and RoboTwin 2.0 [8]. These works score agents with criteria written for demonstration-trained policies; whether the criteria verify only what the instruction asks is rarely examined on its own, and we measure how this gap enters the score of self-improving agent. Self-improving agents and the feedback their learners see. In digital domains, programs are evolved against automatic evaluators [23, 34], agents reflect on textual feedback [28, 36], skills are verified in game world [31], and code is revised against tests [33]. Embodied systems differ in how much of the success criteria their learners or agents see. Some give only success or keep the grader isolated [21, 27]; others add rule descriptions with coarse feedback [10], published scoring tables and partial numeric thresholds [13, 14, 18], formal goal predicates [32], or the source code of the verifier [3]. In RATs, the verifier reads goal predicates and ground truth while the policy writers side is filtered [35]. In these systems the amount of criteria information is mostly fixed by design rather than varied as an experimental factor. The closest comparison is an ablation of EmbodiedEvo between task descriptions alone and descriptions with the wiki, but both arms are judged by the original criteria [18]. We treat exposure as the variable and test what it gains under second set of criteria. Specification gaming and benchmark validity. Optimizing proxy diverges from the intended objective [2, 30], with measurable effects of reward misspecification [24]. Language agents exploit tests and evaluators they can inspect [5, 37], and agentic benchmarks need checks of their own validity [16, 40]. Where rulebased criteria are missing, success is judged by VLMs [11] or by autonomous real-world evaluation [39]. Building on these studies, we further show that on embodied benchmarks the act of reading the criteria turns the gap between criteria and instruction into score, and we measure this share with counterfactual criteria that score the same instructions.

sections.title: 3 Preliminaries and Study Design
sections.content: This section describes the controlled study we use to analyze what self-improving embodied agent learns from the success criteria. The study compares two settings of one loop, w/ CE and w/o CE, and answers three questions: where exposure raises the score under the original criteria, whether the advantage holds when the criteria change, and whether the library carries over to new tasks and benchmarks. We describe in turn the loop and its two settings, criteria-limited tasks, instruction-faithful criteria, and the evaluation protocol.

3.2 Criteria-limited Tasks
We call a task criteria-limited if 𝐶𝜏 disagrees with 𝑆𝜏 on some trajectories, either by rejecting a trajectory 𝑆𝜏
accepts or by accepting one 𝑆𝜏 rejects (criteria looser than the instruction); all other tasks are faithful. Such
tasks appear in every benchmark we examined, RoboDojo, LIBERO [20] (whose instructions and goals
LIBERO-PRO keeps), RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0 [8], and their disagreements fall into a few kinds.
The criteria may ask for more than the instruction states, such as an order, a count or an end state: in
RoboDojo, press_by_number requires a button protocol its instruction never gives. They may be stricter
than the instruction needs, such as an unstated tolerance for an object resting on another in LIBERO.
They may contradict the instruction, as in a LIBERO task that asks to stack a bowl on the front bowl
while its criteria require the back one. Or they may verify less than the instruction asks: in RoboTwin 2.0,
shake_bottle_horizontally succeeds once the bottle is lifted.
sections.content: 4 We rewrite criteria and re-judge episodes on RoboDojo only. Its criteria report score and stages besides success, so an exposed learner reads the most complete information there, and we compared the criteria of all of its tasks with their instructions; rewriting the criteria of other benchmarks and repeating these experiments on them is left to future work. We distinguish seven types: hidden rules, hard thresholds, timing and irreversible events, criteria defects, extra end states, loose criteria, and contradictions. In RoboDojo, after manual review of every task, the 20 criteria-limited tasks have 26 variants, and hidden rules and hard thresholds are the most common types. Criteria-limited is defined with respect to the instruction the agent receives at reset; the RoboDojo website publishes part of these rules in its task descriptions and scoring tables.

sections.title: 3.3 Instruction-faithful Criteria
sections.content: For each criteria-limited task we rewrite only the criteria code, never the instruction, and leave the original repository untouched: hidden rules are removed or relaxed, defects fixed, hard thresholds relaxed to what still clearly satisfies the instruction, loose criteria tightened where the simulator state can detect the difference, and the return of both arms kept. The two criteria judged the same episodes independently, and every episode whose verdict flipped was checked by hand without finding misjudgment by the new criteria. Each evaluation episode is then judged by both criteria, giving SRorig and SRfaith. Since both criteria score the same instruction on the same episode, any difference between the two success rates comes from what the criteria verify, not from behavior. 𝐶faith is ours and serves as proxy for 𝑆𝜏; we discuss this in section 5.

sections.title: 3.4 Experiment Settings and Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: To isolate the effect of exposure, the two settings of each comparison use the same actor, primitives, round budget and development layouts. The 25 learned tasks comprise 16 criteria-limited and 9 faithful tasks, grouped in advance by whether their criteria were rewritten; Appendix A.4 lists the tasks. Development uses layouts 04 of seed 1 and testing layouts 019 of seed 0. We report the success rate (SR) and compare settings layout by layout. All experiments use the same actor and learner. To reuse libraries, we distill the libraries of ten source tasks into one shared library and apply it to disjoint target tasks, in RoboDojo and on two further benchmarks with aligned primitives. We use three simulated benchmarks with different roles. RoboDojo is the main benchmark: its rule-based criteria report score and stages, and all three questions are answered on it. LIBERO-PRO is single-arm tabletop benchmark where zero-shot success is already near the ceiling; it tests whether transfer still has room at high scores. RoboCasa365 has household kitchen scenes and the lowest zero-shot scores; it tests cross-benchmark experience and also hosts in-benchmark learning.

sections.title: 4 Experiments and Analysis
sections.content: We test three hypotheses: H1. Exposure raises the score only on tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction (section 4.1). H2. If exposure teaches the verifier rather than the task, its lead shrinks or reverses when the same episodes are judged by instruction-faithful criteria (section 4.2.1), and each exposed library scores best under whichever criteria its learner read (section 4.2.2). H3. What exposure adds does not carry over to new tasks or benchmarks (section 4.3).

sections.title: 4.1 Exposure under the Original Criteria
sections.content: We first judge the benchmarks way, by the original criteria, which are also the criteria the exposed learner reads.

sections.title: 4.1.1 Success-only versus Exposed Self-Improvement
sections.content: Setup. We learn one library per task and setting on the 25 learned tasks (16 criteria-limited, 9 faithful), over five rounds on five development layouts, and test each library on layouts 019 of seed 0 against the empty library. The two groups were fixed before any result was seen. 5 Figure 3 Development success by round, on the 16 criteria-limited and the 9 faithful tasks. Dashed: w/ CE; solid: w/o CE; round 0 is the empty library. On criteria-limited tasks both settings start at 6% and part in round 1 (40% against 28%); after that the success-only learner barely moves and ends at 31%, against 55% with exposure. On faithful tasks the success-only learner is ahead through round 4 and both end above 90% (91% and 95%); its lead, at most 16 points, is close to the 14-point gap of round 0 (66% against 52%), where both run the same empty library. Results. Table 1 and figure 3 show three patterns. First, learning from success alone doubles success, from 24.6% to 47.8%, and reading the criteria adds another 14.2 points (62.0%). Second, this extra gain comes from the criteria-limited tasks: on faithful tasks the two settings are level (83.3% and 80.6%), while on criteria-limited tasks exposure leads, 51.6% against 27.8%. Third, among criteria-limited tasks the lead depends on whether an unstated rule shows in failed episodes: in build_tower the leftover blocks reveal it and both settings reach 20/20, whereas the button protocol of press_by_number, blue pressed twice and between the two red groups, never shows, and the success-only learner never finds it.

sections.title: 4.1.2 Synthesis
sections.content: Exposure pays off only where the criteria ask for more than the instruction. Richer feedback is often assumed to make self-improvement better. Our results show condition: when the criteria verify what the instruction says, success alone tells the learner what the task requires, and what remains, reliable procedure, is learned equally well in both settings. Exposure helps only with rules that the instruction omits and that failures do not reveal. The advantage of exposure measures the benchmark as much as the agent. Because it comes from what the instruction leaves out, the gain of exposure grows with the gap between benchmarks instructions and its criteria. Some of what the criteria reveal is legitimate task knowledge, but it belongs in the instruction: benchmarks that state in the instruction what their criteria verify (counts, order, end states, the reset of the arms) and release versioned criteria with comparison against the instructions would let self-improvement be compared on the task alone.

sections.title: 4.2.3 Synthesis and Implications
sections.content: Exposure makes self-improvement fit the criteria rather than learn the instructed task. higher score from reading the criteria is commonly taken as faster learning of the task. learner that reads the criteria, however, revises the library until it passes the verifier it reads, so the library learns the task only as far as the criteria agree with the instruction. Under instruction-faithful criteria the exposed library loses successes that the success-only library gains, and each exposed library scores best only under the criteria it read: on press_by_number it solves all 20 layouts under 𝐶orig and none under 𝐶faith, and the library that read 𝐶faith solves 65.0% of its test episodes under 𝐶faith but 13.5% under 𝐶orig. 7 Self-improvement should therefore be measured without exposure by default, with the success rate under instruction-faithful criteria reported alongside: robot in the real world has no criteria code, so the part of gain that survives change of criteria is the part to expect there. Exposure changes what the learner writes down. learner that reads the criteria can explain failure by the condition it violated, so its experience is phrased in the terms of one verifier; learner that sees only success has to find physical cause, and its rules are closer to regularities of the robot. About third of the exposed memory entries cite the criteria code, and none of the success-only ones do.

sections.title: 4.3.3 Synthesis and Implications
sections.content: What exposure adds is specific to the task it was learned on. One might expect the setting that scores higher on its own tasks to transfer better. It does not: the lead of exposure disappears on target tasks. Exposed experience carries the conditions and precision needed to pass one tasks criteria, which become noise or overhead elsewhere, whereas rules about the gripper hold across tasks. Experience transfers where the bottleneck is shared. Within benchmark the robot, the scenes and perception stay the same, and learned rules carry over. Across benchmarks the general part of the experience is already covered by the targets prompt, while what the target lacks has no counterpart in the source, so the transferred skills go unused; experience gathered on the target benchmark, even on other tasks, addresses its own bottleneck and helps.

sections.title: 5 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: The instruction-faithful criteria are ours, and the feedback is simulated. 𝐶faith serves as our proxy for the success the instruction asks for, 𝑆𝜏. Neither settings libraries saw the rewritten criteria when they were written; rules and types were fixed in advance; second seed was judged independently and every flipped episode checked. Still, only RoboDojos criteria were rewritten, and success-only feedback in simulation is cleaner than the success human or VLM reports for robot in the real world, which has no criteria code. Next steps are an independent review, released criteria code, rewritten criteria for second benchmark, and VLM success detection in place of the simulators success [11]. Exposure is studied at two levels, as current systems implement it. Most existing systems sit at intermediate levels (rule descriptions, published scoring tables, partial thresholds), which we did not study separately. next step is to expose these levels one at time and measure how the gain under 𝐶orig, and its loss under 𝐶faith, grow with what the learner reads. Samples are small and the mechanisms are inferred. Each task has 20 test layouts, so quantitative claims use pooled results and single tasks are described only qualitatively; and distillation variance was not estimated. The accounts of what exposure writes into the library, of what carries over and of how the actor uses transferred libraries rest on entry text, skill calls and action statistics, not on ablations. Next steps are repeated distillations and ablations that remove or swap individual entries, such as the re-measuring entries of the distilled w/ CE library or the memory entries of translated library.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we studied what self-improving embodied agent learns when it reads the success criteria, by comparing one self-improvement loop with and without Criteria Exposure, under the benchmarks own and instruction-faithful criteria, and on new tasks and benchmarks. Our results show that selfimprovement from success alone is real and survives change of criteria, whereas the score that Criteria Exposure adds comes mainly from satisfying the criteria that were read: it appears only where the criteria and the instruction disagree, disappears under instruction-faithful criteria, and across benchmarks neither the exposed nor the success-only library gives clear gain, while only in-benchmark experience helps. These findings provide more careful reading of reported self-improvement gains on embodied benchmarks and practical guidance for measuring them: use the feedback robot receives in the real world, and judge by criteria that verify what the instruction says. robot in the real world never sees its verifier; the agent we measure should not either.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: A.1 Experimental protocol Benchmark. RoboDojos simulation track uses dual-arm ARX-X5 with RGB observations only; its 42 tasks span five capability dimensions. The 20 tasks on which the zero-shot actor solves fewer than half of the episodes of the official evaluation seed, with five stronger ones, make the 25 compared tasks  (table 4)  . Every run uses one version of RoboDojo  (Table 3)  ; task source, criteria, leaderboard script and evaluation layouts are identical file by file across the checkouts we compare. Conditions. The actors model, primitives and prompt are the same in every condition. The learner with Criteria Exposure reads the criteria code, each episodes score and its passed stages; the one without sees full trajectories and success only. All conditions are compared over five rounds of improvement (rounds 05). The groups (Appendix B) rest on reading the code, the learners diagnoses and the failed rollouts. Layouts. Development reruns layouts 04 of official evaluation seed 1 every round; the test layouts are layouts 019 of seed 0 (500 episodes per condition), which no learner sees. Statistics. Development batches are noisy: rerunning one library on one layout changes the verdict in 4% of cases, and the two round-0 batches of the same empty library differ in at least 13% of episodes. We therefore draw conclusions from the test layouts and pooled curves, and read single-task development curves only qualitatively. A.2 Implementation and settings Actor. GPT-6 Astra writes one code cell per MLLM call against PyRUA-Leans frozen robo API [29]: RGB perception (SAM 3 [7] and multi-view measurement) and motion primitives, with no VLA policy, depth or simulator state. The library is installed as package library/: cells import its skills, and its live memory entries are appended to the prompt. Library. skill is function of robo that imports only standard modules, numpy and other library modules, does no I/O and returns {"ok": ..., "why": ..., ...}. memory entry is ## {task}-<stage>-<nnn> followed by stage, symptom, applies, do, status and evidence. tasks library holds at most 40,000 characters, all of which the actor reads. Learner. Claude Code reads the session, the tasks dev runs, the API source and, with Criteria Exposure, the tasks criteria; it writes only the candidate library, its verification rollouts and its notes. Without Criteria Exposure, criteria, scores and stages are removed from the evidence. Acceptance and rollback. candidate may change only the tasks own directory, must keep every memory entry identifier, must cite judged rollout or dev batch for each entry newly marked dev_verified, and must pass the static skill rules and the size limit; none of this looks at success, and no candidate was refused. The active revision rolls back to the best earlier complete batch when complete batch has two or more fewer successes; ties go to the batch that passed more stages, and batch with an episode lost to infrastructure neither triggers rollback nor becomes the best. A.3 Evaluation details The 25 learned tasks are grouped by whether their criteria were rewritten. Layouts that the benchmark marks unstable are replaced by the next layout in the official order. Under dual judging an episode ends early only when both criteria have reached verdict, so neither verdict is truncated. sections.title: B Comparing Criteria with Instructions in RoboDojo
sections.content: Criteria mechanism. RoboDojo criteria are sequences of stages: check stages in order, final_check at termination, and trigger_check, evaluated only at the step its condition becomes true; query requires exact counts and fails the episode for good once count is exceeded; conditions nest with alternating AND and OR. Of the 42 tasks, 33 require both arms to return within 15 cm and 20 of home, while only 5 instructions ask for reset. Method. For each task we compare gen_instruction, run_reward, get_score and the configuration, grade the severity as high, medium or low, and confirm by hand; the review is mainly static reading of the code. Types. The type names are ours. Hidden rule: the criteria verify conditions the instruction does not state (order, counts, relative position), e.g. the button protocol of press_by_number or the tile to draw in make_kong. Hard threshold: the tolerance is stricter than clearly satisfying the instruction requires, e.g. 97% of the liquid in pour_liquid_into_cup. Timing, event triggers and irreversibility: verification at one step only, or permanent failure once an event happens, e.g. pouring judged only when the bottle returns upright; third press in press_by_number. Criteria defect: the criteria code or an asset annotation is wrong, e.g. mug 14 in hang_mugs_random, the bug in solve_equation. Extra end state: an end state the instruction does not mention, e.g. in make_toast the two remaining slices must stay on the bread shelf. Loose criteria: trajectories that skip the action the instruction asks for are accepted, e.g. sweep_blocks accepts blocks picked up without the broom. Contradiction: the criteria require the opposite of the instruction, e.g. in classify_objects_by_language the categories are named after asset folders, so chocolate bunny counts as wooden toy. 14 Counts. 23 tasks are consistent and 19 inconsistent (hidden rule 9, hidden rule and hard threshold 5, hard threshold 3, contradiction 1, defect 1); with solve_equation, whose criteria have bug, 20 tasks and 26 variants are criteria-limited. By type, at medium or high severity: hidden rule 13, hard threshold 13, timing and events 10, defect 9, extra end state 5, loose criteria 4, contradiction 3. Other typical cases are make_kong (a tile must be drawn) and build_tower (only one configuration is accepted). Published rules. The task descriptions and scoring tables on the RoboDojo website publish part of these rules, for example the button order of press_by_number; the recipes of EmbodiedEvo and HexaShell come from there [13, 18]. sections.title: F What Exposure Writes into the Library
sections.content: Setup. We classify the memory entries of the ten source libraries of the RoboDojo transfer (section G), for both settings, by whether they cite the criteria code, and compare entries that the two settings wrote from the same source failures. Results. Two patterns emerge. First, an exposed library writes its experience in the language of the criteria: 19 of the 55 exposed entries cite the criteria code (47% of the characters), and none of the 53 success-only entries does. Figure 6 shows three exposed entries: the grip-and-pull of the button cap in swap_blocks and the ban on sweeping in sweep_blocks_random, which cite the criteria code, and the hidden protocol of press_by_number, which restates the order of the checks in words. Such entries fail under 𝐶faith and have to be removed for transfer: distilling on-10 dropped 9 entries on what the benchmark checks. Second, learner that cannot see the criteria has to find physical cause. From the same source failures, in which the gripper closes on nothing, the success-only learner traced the cause to half-open gripper whose fingers KEEP moves close again, and wrote pass OPEN on every move of an empty gripper; the exposed learner recorded the symptom and kept formula that in effect half-opens the gripper (figure 7). Not all exposed entries concern the verifier, though: some carry information the instruction should state, such as the pen orientation in fill_pen_holder. 18 press_by_number, press_by_number-manipulate-001 (learner w/ CE) do: Press in exactly this order: LEFT red xN_left (left arm) -> BLUE once (right arm) -> MIDDLE red xN_middle (right arm) -> BLUE once more -> ... Blue is pressed exactly TWICE, never more. ... evidence: task checks in order: repeat(button0 below 0.5 / above 0.9) num0; button2 below 0.5; ... swap_blocks, swap_blocks-verify-001 (learner w/ CE) do: the benchmark judges after every action, in order: lift block 1 -> block 1 on the empty mat -> cap pressed below 50% of its travel -> cap seen back ABOVE 90% -> ... push alone ... does not bring the cap back above 90%: the fingers must grip the cap and pull it up. sweep_blocks_random, sweep_blocks_random-manipulate-001 (learner w/ CE) do: do NOT pick up, hand over or sweep with the broom. The benchmark only checks, in one action: every objects centre inside the dustpans bin, dustpan not lifted and upright, brooms > dustpans + 0.10 m, both arms home. Carry the objects in by hand: ... Figure 6 Exposed entries are written in the language of the criteria. Excerpts of three memory entries of the exposed source libraries, verbatim (. . . marks elisions). The first fixes an order of presses that the instruction does not state, with the verification order of the criteria as evidence; the second turns verified condition (above 90%) into grip-and-pull of the button cap; the third tells the actor not to use the broom the instruction names (pick up the broom, hand it over to the right hand), because the verifier never looks at it. All three are marked dev_verified; the on-10 distillation dropped all three.

sections.title: G Library Transfer
sections.content: To reuse libraries across tasks, we distill the libraries of ten source tasks into one shared library and apply it to disjoint target tasks; entries of exposed libraries that are tied to the criteria are removed during distillation. Across benchmarks, the libraries are applied on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 with primitives aligned to those of RoboDojo (Appendix J); within RoboCasa365 we also run both settings of the loop and distill one library from each, as reference for in-benchmark experience. In RoboDojo, the success-only and exposed libraries off-10 and on-10 take ten learned tasks as sources and are applied to ten target tasks that no source covers  (table 2)  ; off-rc10 and on-rc10 are distilled within RoboCasa365 from both settings of the loop. The case study is in Appendix H. Brief. The distiller receives, for each source task, the library as the actor read it in the last evaluated revision (retired entries removed), the learners last diagnosis and the development successes per round, and the robot API source; it does not see the target tasks and is told not to look for them. It writes memory entries of at most 12,000 characters in the source format (stage, symptom, applies, do, evidence) and at most two skill modules of 15,000 characters. Every entry must state general rule, name no task, object, dimension or goal configuration in do, and cite evidence from at least two source tasks, or from one task where it decided between failing and succeeding rounds, flagged as single-task rule; separate notes file, not given to the actor, records the source of every entry and what was left out. The two briefs differ in one passage on the learners: they never saw the benchmarks judging code (w/o CE) against rule that only describes how one task is judged (its thresholds, its check order) does not transfer; keep what is about perception and manipulation (w/ CE). Process. Each library is distilled in one session by Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (effort high). Before evaluation, every library is checked for the character limits, the entry fields, source task names, and that each library function it names exists and parses; skills are exercised against stub robot with the real API signatures, not in simulation. Results. Table 9 gives the ten target tasks. Off-10 leads on-10 by 9 episodes, and most of the difference sits in insert_tubes and solve_equation (Appendix H). Why Cross-benchmark Libraries Help Little Setup. The libraries off-10 and on-10 of Appendix are translated to the prompt and primitives of LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365; off-rc10 and on-rc10 are distilled from RoboCasa365 tasks disjoint from its ten target tasks. At the start of an episode the library is placed in the actors working directory: skill runs only if the actors code imports it, while the memory entries are appended to the prompt. We count the episodes whose code imports or calls skill. Results. Three reasons explain why neither settings library gives clear gain across benchmarks. First, the translated skills are almost never called. Even within RoboDojo only 5% (off-10) and 20.5% (on-10) of the episodes call skill. None of the 200 RoboCasa365 episodes with off-10 or on-10 calls one, and on LIBERO-PRO only 5 and 12 of 60 episodes do. The libraries distilled within RoboCasa365 are 21 called in 158 of 200 episodes, mostly their perception functions for two-view localization and joint margins. Across benchmarks, the memory entries appended to the prompt are the only part of translated library the actor uses. Second, what the translated libraries hold is not what the targets need. They cover grasping from above, placing and withdrawing at table; translation removed the content about two arms, hand-overs and the table geometry, and found no source experience for moving the base. Most of the ten RoboCasa365 target tasks open doors, turn knobs, pull drawers or reach into racks, and need the base to move. The libraries distilled within RoboCasa365 cover exactly these: moving the base in front of door, swinging hinged part about its axis, approaching under an overhang, and recovering when the arm is near its joint limits. The perception experience does not carry either: the millimetre-level precision learned in RoboDojo does not hold on RoboCasa365, where the measured height of an object top is off by 28 cm. Third, LIBERO-PRO leaves little room. With the aligned primitives, the empty library already solves 188 of 200 episodes on the four swap suites, and only six of the 40 tasks are not solved on every seed. On four of these six every library solves 810 of 10 seeds; the differences come from two tasks, putting book into the back compartment of caddy (empty, off-10, on-10: 6 / 8 / 5 of 10) and putting mug into the microwave and closing it (2 / 3 / 3). The same library solves different numbers on the two halves of the seeds (empty 21 / 24, off-10 22 / 26, on-10 25 / 21, of 30 each), spread larger than the gain of any library. Interpretation. Transfer helps where source and target share the bottleneck. Within RoboDojo the robot, the table and perception stay the same, and off-10 gains on target tasks. Across benchmarks, the general part of the experience (grasping, placing, finishing) is what the targets prompt and the actor already handle, and what the target lacks, moving the base and operating articulated parts, has no counterpart in the source. library distilled on the target benchmark, even from other tasks, covers that bottleneck, is called in most episodes, and helps. Two caveats apply: skill that is never called does not mean the library has no effect, since its memory entries are always in the prompt; and we evaluated one way of translating library, not variants such as skills without memory. Cross-benchmark Primitive Alignment With the aligned primitives, the empty library solves 41, 47, 50 and 50 of 50 episodes on the four LIBEROPRO swap suites (10, goal, object, spatial), against 36, 45, 44 and 39 for the published PyRUA-Lean [29]; on RoboCasa365 it solves 55/90 atomic and 54/160 composite episodes, against 59/90 and 32/160 published.
